blocks.text: Every NumPy array has to start somewhere, and that somewhere is always one of a small set of constructor functions. Learn what each one is actually for, and you stop guessing every time you sit down to write code that touches data.

Think about setting up a fresh spreadsheet. Sometimes you already have numbers you want to paste in. Sometimes you want a completely blank grid of a known size that you will fill in later. Sometimes you want every cell pre filled with the same starting value, like zero, so you can add to it as you go. NumPy hands you a dedicated tool for each of these situations, and this lesson walks through every one of them.
1. Introduction

Before you touch a single machine learning model, you are going to create arrays. Lots of them. Weight matrices need to start somewhere before training nudges their values. Placeholder buffers need to exist before a loop fills them in. Synthetic test data needs to be generated before you can sanity check a function. Every one of those moments comes down to picking the right constructor.

The constructors in this lesson fall into a few natural families: ones that build an array out of Python data you already have, ones that build a blank array of a chosen shape, ones that build a sequence of numbers following a rule, ones that build identity or diagonal matrices, and ones that copy the shape of an array you already made. Knowing which family you need cuts your decision down from a dozen function names to just one or two.

blocks.title: Two habits worth building now
blocks.content: After you create any array, get in the habit of printing its shape and its dtype. Almost every confusing bug involving array creation traces back to one of those two things being different from what you expected.

blocks.text: 2. Creating Arrays From Data You Already Have

The most common starting point is data you already have sitting in a plain Python list. The function that turns a list into an array is np.array(), and how it behaves depends entirely on the shape of the list you hand it.
2.1 A Flat List Becomes a 1D Array
Pass np.array() a plain flat list of numbers and you get back a 1D array, one row of values with no nesting.

code.content:
import numpy as np

scores = np.array([88, 92, 79, 95, 84])
print(scores)        # [88 92 79 95 84]
print(scores.shape)  # (5,)
print(scores.dtype)  # int64 on most systems

blocks.text: NumPy looks at every value in the list, figures out one common dtype that can hold all of them, and stores the whole thing as one contiguous block of memory. That contiguous block is exactly why NumPy math runs so much faster than looping over a plain Python list.

blocks.alt: A Python list of numbers turning into a 1D NumPy array
blocks.caption: A flat list has no nesting, so it becomes a single row array.

blocks.text: 2.2 A Nested List Becomes a 2D Array
Hand np.array() a list of lists instead, and as long as every inner list is the same length, you get back a proper 2D array. Each inner list becomes one row.

code.content:
grades = np.array([
    [88, 92, 79],
    [95, 84, 90],
    [71, 65, 88],
])
print(grades.shape)  # (3, 3), 3 rows and 3 columns
print(grades[1])     # [95 84 90], the second row

blocks.text: This is the pattern you will use constantly to load a small batch of tabular data, a mini image, or a handful of feature vectors straight into a real 2D array. Once every row is the same length, NumPy is happy to lay the whole thing out as one solid rectangular grid.

blocks.alt: A nested Python list with equal length rows turning into a 2D array
blocks.caption: Equal length rows let NumPy build one clean rectangular grid.

blocks.text: 2.3 Uneven Rows and the Object Dtype Trap

Now break the pattern. If the inner lists are not all the same length, NumPy cannot lay them out as a rectangle anymore. Modern NumPy versions will still build something, but instead of a fast numeric array, you get a 1D array of dtype object, where each element is just a reference back to the original Python list.

code.content:
messy = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5]], dtype=object)
print(messy.shape)  # (2,), NOT (2, 3)
print(messy.dtype)  # object
print(messy[0])     # [1, 2, 3], a plain Python list, not a fast array row

blocks.title: This is usually a bug, not a feature
blocks.content: An object dtype array gives up every performance benefit NumPy exists for. Every element is a boxed Python object, math on it falls back to slow per element Python loops, and most NumPy functions either error out on it or silently do the wrong thing. If you ever see dtype object show up where you expected numbers, go check your row lengths first. That mismatch is almost always the cause.

blocks.text: The fix is almost always to pad the short rows to a common length before building the array, or to keep the data as a genuine Python list of lists until you know every row matches.

blocks.alt: Uneven nested list rows falling back to a slow object dtype array
blocks.caption: Rows of different lengths cannot form a rectangle, so NumPy falls back to a loose object array.

blocks.text: 3. Shape Only Constructors

Sometimes you do not have any data yet. You just know the shape you need, and you want NumPy to hand you a blank array of that shape so you can fill it in yourself, usually inside a loop or before running a computation that writes into it in place.
3.1 zeros, ones and full
np.zeros(shape) gives you an array of the given shape filled with zero everywhere. np.ones(shape) does the same thing but fills with one. np.full(shape, value) lets you pick any fill value at all.

code.content:
zeros_row = np.zeros(5)             # [0. 0. 0. 0. 0.]
ones_grid = np.ones((2, 3))          # a 2 by 3 grid of ones
filled = np.full((2, 3), 7)          # a 2 by 3 grid, every cell holding 7
print(zeros_row.dtype)               # float64 by default

blocks.text: Notice that np.zeros and np.ones default to a float dtype even though the values look like whole numbers. If you specifically need integers, pass dtype=int and NumPy will honor it.

items: np.zeros is the classic choice for an accumulator you plan to add values into.
np.ones shows up constantly as a starting bias vector or a mask that starts fully on.
np.full is handy any time your starting value is not zero or one, like pre filling a distance matrix with infinity.

blocks.alt: Four small boxes representing zeros, ones, full and empty as shape only constructors
blocks.caption: Four shape only constructors, each choosing a different starting fill.

blocks.text: 3.2 empty and Why It Lies to You

np.empty(shape) looks like it belongs right next to zeros and ones, but it behaves very differently. It asks the operating system for a block of memory of the right size and hands it straight back to you, without writing anything into it first.

blocks.title: np.empty does NOT initialize memory
blocks.content: The values you see are whatever bytes happened to already be sitting in that patch of memory, left over from some earlier program. They are not zero, they are not random in any useful sense, they are just garbage. Never read from an array created with np.empty before you have written real values into every single cell. Its only real use is as a small speed optimization when you already know your code is about to overwrite every element anyway, for example right before a loop that fills every index.

blocks.text: In practice, reach for np.zeros unless you have a specific, measured reason to skip the zero fill step. The tiny speed gain from np.empty is rarely worth the risk of accidentally reading uninitialized memory.

blocks.alt: np.empty allocating memory without clearing it, leaving garbage values behind
blocks.caption: Uninitialized memory means whatever was already there shows up as your array values.

blocks.text: 4. Range Like Constructors
The next family builds a sequence of numbers automatically, the way Python's built in range() does, except it hands you back a real NumPy array instead of a lazy iterator.
4.1 arange: Stepping by a Fixed Amount

np.arange(start, stop, step) gives you every value from start up to but not including stop, moving forward by step each time. It is the direct NumPy cousin of Python's range, and it also accepts float steps, which range does not.

blocks.title: Floating point steps can drift
blocks.content: Because arange works by repeatedly adding the step, tiny floating point rounding errors can occasionally make the array end one element longer or shorter than you expected. If the exact count of points matters more than the exact step size, linspace is the safer choice, covered next.

blocks.alt: arange stepping forward by a fixed increment from a start value up to a stop value
blocks.caption: arange keeps adding the same step until it reaches the stop value.

blocks.text: 4.2 linspace: Fixing the Count Instead

np.linspace(start, stop, num) flips the question around. Instead of telling NumPy the step size, you tell it exactly how many points you want, and it works out the step size for you so those points land evenly between start and stop, with both endpoints included by default.

That looks similar to the arange example above, but the difference in intent matters. With arange you are saying "keep going in steps of this size." With linspace you are saying "give me exactly this many points, spaced evenly, I do not care what the step size works out to." Any time you are building an x axis for a plot, sampling a range for a test, or generating evenly spaced probe values, you almost certainly know the count you want, which makes linspace the right tool.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation","Reach for"],"rows":[["You know the exact step size you want","np.arange"],["You know the exact number of points you want","np.linspace"],["You need the endpoint included with certainty","np.linspace"],["Floating point step drift would be a problem","np.linspace"]]}

blocks.alt: linspace fixing the count of points first and spacing them evenly between two endpoints
blocks.caption: linspace starts from a chosen count and spaces points evenly to fit it.

blocks.text: 5. Identity and Diagonal Helpers

Linear algebra work leans on two special shapes constantly: the identity matrix and the plain diagonal matrix. NumPy gives each one its own dedicated constructor instead of making you build it by hand.
5.1 eye: Identity Matrices
np.eye(n) builds an n by n square matrix with ones running down the main diagonal and zeros everywhere else. That is the identity matrix, the matrix equivalent of multiplying by one.

You will meet identity matrices constantly when working through matrix multiplication rules, regularization terms, or just needing a neutral starting point that leaves other matrices unchanged when multiplied against it.

blocks.alt: np.eye producing a square identity matrix with ones on the diagonal
blocks.caption: eye builds a square matrix of ones down the diagonal and zeros elsewhere.

blocks.text: 5.2 diag: Diagonal Matrices

np.diag() is more flexible. Give it a 1D vector, and it builds a square matrix with your values placed along the diagonal and zeros everywhere else. Give it a 2D matrix instead, and it does the reverse, pulling the diagonal values back out into a 1D vector.

code.content:
values = np.array([4, 7, 2])
square = np.diag(values)
print(square)
# [[4 0 0]
#  [0 7 0]
#  [0 0 2]]

back_out = np.diag(square)
print(back_out)  # [4 7 2]

blocks.text: This comes in handy any time you need to scale different features by different amounts, since multiplying by a diagonal matrix scales each dimension independently, or any time you need to quickly build a covariance style matrix for a toy example.

blocks.alt: np.diag placing a vector of values along the diagonal of a square matrix
blocks.caption: diag turns a vector into a square matrix with those values down the diagonal.

blocks.text: 6. Copying Another Array's Shape

You often already have an array sitting around, maybe your actual training data or a previous result, and you want a fresh array with the exact same shape and dtype, just filled with a different starting value. Writing out the shape by hand works, but it is easy to get wrong, especially once shapes get complicated. The like family of constructors solves this directly.
6.1 zeros_like, ones_like and full_like

code.content:
data = np.array([[1.5, 2.5, 3.5], [4.5, 5.5, 6.5]])

zeros_copy = np.zeros_like(data)   # same shape and dtype, all zero
ones_copy = np.ones_like(data)     # same shape and dtype, all one
full_copy = np.full_like(data, 9)  # same shape and dtype, all 9

blocks.text: Each of these reads the shape and dtype straight off the array you pass in, so you never have to type out the shape yourself or risk a typo that leaves you with a mismatched array later. This shows up all the time when you need a mask, an accumulator, or a placeholder that has to line up exactly with an existing batch of data.

blocks.alt: zeros_like and ones_like copying the shape of an existing array
blocks.caption: The like family copies shape and dtype from an existing array automatically.

blocks.text: 7. Choosing the Right Constructor
With this many options, the real skill is not memorizing every function signature, it is recognizing which situation you are in fast enough that reaching for the right constructor becomes automatic.

Boiled down to the four questions you will ask yourself most often, the choice usually collapses to one clear answer within a couple of seconds.

blocks.text: 8. Worked Example: Building a Synthetic Dataset

Put a few of these constructors together and you can build a small synthetic dataset from scratch in just a few lines, which is exactly what you will do constantly when testing a new function before pointing it at real data.
Say you want ten evenly spaced input readings between 0 and 5, alongside a matching label column that starts out unlabeled until you fill it in later.

code.content:
import numpy as np

# 10 evenly spaced readings between 0 and 5, count matters here, so linspace
readings = np.linspace(0, 5, 10)

# a matching column of labels, starts at zero until real labels get assigned
labels = np.zeros(10, dtype=int)

# stack them together into one 10 by 2 dataset, column 0 is the reading, column 1 is the label
dataset = np.column_stack([readings, labels])
print(dataset.shape)  # (10, 2)
print(dataset[:3])
# [[0.         0.        ]
#  [0.55555556 0.        ]
#  [1.11111111 0.        ]]

blocks.text: Now imagine you also want a small identity style weight matrix to start a toy transformation with no effect yet, plus a second batch shaped exactly like your first one, just to run a parallel experiment.

code.content:
starting_weights = np.eye(2)          # a neutral 2 by 2 starting transform
second_batch = np.full_like(dataset, -1.0)  # same shape as dataset, flagged as unfilled with -1
print(starting_weights)
# [[1. 0.]
#  [0. 1.]]
print(second_batch.shape)  # (10, 2), matches dataset exactly

blocks.text: Notice how each constructor did exactly one small job: linspace fixed the count of readings, zeros gave a placeholder label column, eye gave a neutral starting transform, and full_like guaranteed the second batch matched the first one's shape without you ever typing the number 10 twice. That is the real payoff of learning this whole family properly, you stop writing shape numbers by hand and start letting NumPy carry them for you.
9. Recap

items: np.array turns existing Python data into an array, and a nested list only becomes a clean 2D array when every row is the same length. Uneven rows fall back to a slow object dtype array, almost always by accident.
np.zeros, np.ones and np.full build a blank array of a chosen shape filled with a chosen value.
np.empty skips initializing memory entirely, so its contents are garbage until you overwrite every cell yourself.
np.arange steps by a fixed amount, while np.linspace fixes the count of evenly spaced points instead, which is usually what you actually want.
np.eye builds an identity matrix, np.diag builds a diagonal matrix from a vector.
np.zeros_like, np.ones_like and np.full_like copy the shape and dtype of an array you already have.

blocks.text: Once these constructors feel automatic, creating the right starting array for any piece of code stops being a decision at all. You will just reach for the one that matches your situation and move on to the actual problem you are trying to solve.
